catalog_quote: [Arnold 2025, sec. 4.1] The word prosodic systems of the Maˈya dialects (Kawe, Laganyan, Wauyai, Salawati, Misool) and Biga are all very similar. Following Remijsen (2001a, 2001b, 2002), who builds on a tonal analysis first proposed in van der Leeden (1993), all these varieties are analysed with both lexical tone and lexical stress. Tone specifications in all languages are almost exclusively culminative (i.e., there is a maximum of on tone per word) and restricted to word‑final syllables. ... QUOTE: Arnold 2025 accepted ms, sec. 4.1 'SYNCHRONY' begins PDF/ms p.13 (line 12 of page) and the deciding sentence 'Stress, on the other hand, falls unpredictably on either the penultimate or final syllable of polysyllabic words in all varieties; in at least Salawati Ma'ya, phonetic correlates of stress are increased duration, less centralised vowels, and increased intensity when compared with unstressed syllables (Remijsen 2001a: 54-68)' is on ms p.14 exactly as quoted; the two '..' in the report elide 'who builds on a tonal analysis first proposed in van der Leeden (1993),' and the tone-example sentences/tables 4-5 -- legitimate ellipses, word…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Laganyan (Legenyem) Ma'ya has lexical (contrastive) stress confined to a two-syllable window at the right edge: each polysyllabic word is stressed on either the penult or the final syllable, unpredictably; this co-exists with a culminative word-final tone contrast (High / Rise / toneless). Corroborated first-hand by Remijsen 2001 (LOT 49) pp.19, 53, 70-71 and his stress-marked Laganyan wordlist (App. A.3).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in either source.
new_statements.exceptions: Strong tendency for penult-stressed words to have identical penult and final vowels; in Laganyan (as in all Ma'ya dialects except Misool) a penult-stressed word cannot bear Rise tone; in the Waigeo dialects (incl. Laganyan) the final vowel of penult-stressed words with open final syllable and identical vowels is apocopated phrase-medially (Arnold Table 8; Remijsen p.19). Remijsen pp.106-107 (for Salawati Ma'ya): final stress occurs only when the penult vowel is /a/; otherwise stress is penultimate. Monosyllables are simply stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical stress on roots (Remijsen p.49: prefixation does not shift stress; function words have variable stress). Arnold's Laganyan forms were recorded 'in a range of different utterance contexts'; apocope conditioned by phrase-medial vs phrase-final position. Remijsen's instrumental stress study (ch.3) is on the Salawati dialect, not Laganyan.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog lege1241 'Legenyem' [lcc] is the variety both modern describers call the Laganyan dialect of Ma'ya (maya1282): Remijsen 2001:15 fn.13 explicitly equates Hartzler's (1978) 'Legenyem' with Laganyan (villages Lupintol, Arway, ?Bew/Beo, Mayalibit Bay, Waigeo); Arnold 2025 uses her own 2023 Laganyan field data. The quoted sentence covers all five Ma'ya dialects plus Biga jointly, with Laganyan named and given its own 'Y' for contrastive penult/final stress in Table 9; Remijsen's instrumental stress measurements are from the Salawati dialect. If the catalog keys Ma'ya (maya1282) separately, this entry is the same prosodic system described at dialect level.

new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the existing statement (Arnold 2025: all Ma'ya dialects incl. Laganyan analysed with both lexical tone and lexical stress, stress unpredictably penultimate or final) and with Remijsen 2001; this deposit is the 2023 Laganyan field data (speaker Arfus Saleo, Lopintol/Waisai) on which Arnold 2025's Laganyan column rests. It adds no new rule, only stress- and tone-marked primary transcriptions. Access note: datashare.ed.ac.uk itself still refuses our network (attempt 1 browser-UA automated download -L on hdl 8573: rc 52 empty reply; attempt 2 --http1.1 on hdl 8591 plus METS/OAI/show=full endpoints: rc 52), so the pages and bitstreams were read from the Internet Archive captures…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is stated anywhere in the deposit: it is primary data (audio + a 56-page scanned handwritten elicitation questionnaire + 463-byte metadata files). The printed template's Phonology section (1.2, pp.5-7) is left blank for Laganyan. Every Laganyan word in the word lists (pp.16-42, recorded in isolation / utterance-final / utterance-medial frames) is transcribed with a stress mark and tone diacritics (acute = High, hacek = Rise, some words annotated 'TONELESS'); the stress mark sits on the penultimate syllable in some words ([ˈgulúm], [ˈmoró], [ˈloló], [ˈpasǐl]) and on the final syllable in others ([lyaˈhán], [maleˈpáp], [aˈlíf]), i.e. the transcription practice presupposes lexically specified stress within the last two syllables plus a final-syllable tone contrast, exactly the analysis Arnold (2025) states in prose.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none marked; only one stress mark per word in the transcriptions
new_statements.exceptions: none (no analytic text); phrase-medial (NEG frame) forms show final-vowel loss in some penult-stressed words (e.g. p.17 16 sky [ˈnalo] ~ NEG frame [ˈna pap hapo]), matching the apocope Arnold 2025 Table 8 and Remijsen 2001:19 describe, but this is my observation of the data, not a statement in the work
new_statements.identity_note: The deposit is explicitly the Laganyan dialect of Ma'ya (ISO lcc, Glottocode lege1241), one speaker, Arfus Saleo (b. 1979, born Lopintol on Mayalibit Bay, Waigeo; recorded in Waisai 1-2 March 2023). The same fieldnotes PDF also carries black-ink Kawe Ma'ya (kawe1240) data from speaker Yuliue Akello (Selpele); only the green-ink entries are Laganyan.
